chunks: Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub, from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Abu Ayyub, from Muhammad ibn Marid, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who made a will to a man and commanded him to free a slave on his behalf for six hundred dirhams from his third. So the executor went and gave the six hundred dirhams to a man to perform Hajj on behalf of the deceased. He said, so Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'I see that the executor should bear the cost of six hundred dirhams from his own wealth, and he should place the six hundred dirhams in what the deceased willed, for a slave.'
Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Fadhl, from Muhammad ibn Urmah al-Qummi, from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Ash'ari, who said:

I said to Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him), 'May I be your ransom, I asked our companions about what I intend to ask you, but I did not find an answer with them, and I have been compelled to ask you. Indeed, Sa'd ibn Sa'd made a will to me, and he willed in his will: 'Perform Hajj for me,' vaguely, without specifying. So what should I do?' He said, 'My answer will come to you in your letter.' So he (peace be upon him) wrote: 'He should perform Hajj as long as he has wealth to carry it.'
ai.seo_question: How should an executor handle a vague will to 'perform Hajj for the deceased' or a specific bequest for freeing a slave if the executor spends the money differently?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights the Shia juristic principle of distinguishing between the specific allocation of funds and the general estate when an executor misinterprets a vague bequest. In the first case, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that the executor bears the cost of the specific act performed (Hajj) while the designated sum remains in the estate for the intended purpose (manumission), ensuring the deceased's specific wish is not nullified by the executor's action. The second case illustrates the flexibility in executing vague commands, where the Imam instructs that the obligation persists as long as the estate retains sufficient wealth, emphasizing the continuity of the deceased's spiritual debt.
